summary:
Allwork.space argues that AI has made corporate real estate forecasting far harder, strengthening the case for flexible workspace as a hedge rather than a replacement for headquarters. The core problem is not that AI will uniformly cut employment, but that adoption rates, productivity effects and workforce composition will vary by industry, company and job category, with uncertain timing. Some firms will automate drafting, research, customer service, coding and administrative processing and need fewer people in those functions; others will use AI to launch products and expand headcount; many will see both, shrinking back office while growing technology, data, governance, sales and client-facing roles.

Traditional property decisions rest on projected headcount, assumed desk ratios and a chosen workplace strategy. AI destabilizes all three inputs. Office leases are long duration commitments, often ten years or more, with significant fit-out spend, dilapidations exposure and infrequent, expensive break clauses. If management cannot predict staffing two years out, committing to a fixed estate for five or ten years is hard to defend.

The piece notes that headcount is only part of the issue. AI changes the nature of work, team balance, security requirements, collaborative space needs and geographic distribution. Professional services firms may cut junior document review while adding data governance, cyber security, model validation and compliance staff. Smaller teams may still demand better collaboration space, secure project rooms and high quality meeting facilities in talent-retaining locations. The result is volatility in space requirements rather than straightforward office market decline, shifting the question from whether an office is needed to how much space, of what specification, in which locations, and for how long.

Flexible workspace converts part of the property exposure from fixed long-term commitment to variable operating cost, letting an employer keep a core office and use flex to absorb expansion, contraction, project teams, new market entry and changing attendance patterns. The author cites Orega's expansion strategy and IWG's results as evidence of momentum behind "generation flex."

claims.claim: AI has made it harder for senior executives to predict how much office space their organization will need over the next two years
Executives say AI makes flexibility in workspace or real-estate solutions more important
AI is likely to moderate labor-driven office demand as adoption accelerates, though effects vary across organizations and occupations
Conventional office leases can run ten years or more, with substantial fit-out expenditure and dilapidations exposure, and break clauses may be infrequent and expensive to exercise
Orega's recent expansion strategy reflects the expectation that flexible space will take a larger share of corporate space
IWG's latest results show commercial momentum behind the 'generation flex' proposition
